examName: Lean Six Sigma Green Belt (IASSC Certified)
tagline: Drive process improvement through the DMAIC method as a Lean Six Sigma Green Belt.

domains.name: Six Sigma and the Lean Enterprise Fundamentals
domains.description: The basics of Six Sigma, Lean principles, the eight wastes, and 5S as the foundation for DMAIC.

domains.name: Define Phase
domains.description: Define the problem, customer requirements, project scope, and the business case for a Six Sigma project.

domains.name: Measure Phase
domains.description: Map and measure the process baseline using statistics, measurement system analysis, and capability.

domains.name: Analyze Phase
domains.description: Identify and validate root causes of variation using inferential statistics and hypothesis testing.

domains.name: Improve Phase
domains.description: Model relationships and identify improvement solutions using regression analysis.

domains.name: Control Phase
domains.description: Sustain improvements with Lean controls, statistical process control, and control plans.

questions.stem: A process is operating at a true Six Sigma level of quality (with the standard 1.5-sigma long-term shift). Approximately how many defects per million opportunities (DPMO) does this represent?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A Six Sigma process accounts for a 1.5-sigma long-term shift, which yields approximately 3.4 defects per million opportunities — the namesake target of the methodology. Why the others are wrong: **A** 66,807 DPMO corresponds to roughly a 3-sigma process; **C** 6,210 DPMO corresponds to about a 4-sigma process; **D** 233 DPMO corresponds to roughly a 5-sigma process, not six.

questions.stem: An improvement team is cataloging activities at a parts warehouse against the eight wastes of Lean. Which two of the following are classic examples of waste? (Select two.)

options.text: Operators walking long distances between storage racks to pick items (motion)
Finished goods piling up far ahead of customer demand (overproduction/inventory)
A standardized 5S layout that keeps tools at the point of use
A pull signal that triggers replenishment only when stock is consumed

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Excess operator movement is the waste of motion, and building product ahead of demand is overproduction that creates inventory waste — both are among Lean's eight wastes (often recalled by DOWNTIME). Why the others are wrong: **C** a 5S point-of-use layout reduces motion waste rather than creating it; **D** a pull signal limits overproduction, so it is a countermeasure to waste, not a waste.

questions.stem: During a 5S event, a team labels every shadow board, paints floor lines for each cart, and creates a designated home for every tool so that anything out of place is immediately obvious. Which S does this activity primarily represent?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Creating a specific, labeled location for every item — 'a place for everything and everything in its place' — is Set in order (Seiton), the second S. Why the others are wrong: **A** Sort removes unneeded items from the area but does not assign locations; **B** Shine is cleaning and inspecting the workspace; **D** Sustain is maintaining the gains through discipline and audits, not the initial organizing step.

questions.stem: Six Sigma frames improvement with the expression Y = f(x). What do Y and the x's represent in this problem-solving strategy?

options.text: Y is the sample size, and the x's are the confidence intervals
Y is the project budget, and the x's are the individual cost line items
Y is a controllable input, and the x's are the uncontrollable outputs
Y is the output or result of interest, and the x's are the input/process variables that drive it

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Y = f(x) says the output Y (the CTQ or result) is a function of the process inputs x; improving Y means finding and controlling the vital few x's that drive it. Why the others are wrong: **A** sample size and confidence intervals are statistical study parameters, not the Y=f(x) model; **B** the relationship is about process variables, not budgeting; **C** it reverses the roles — Y is the output and the x's are inputs, not the other way around.

questions.stem: A Green Belt gathers customer complaints, survey verbatims, and call-center transcripts, then translates them into specific, measurable product requirements. Which Define-phase activity best describes turning these inputs into requirements?

options.text: Translating the Voice of the Customer (VOC) into Critical-to-Quality (CTQ) characteristics
Calculating the rolled throughput yield (RTY) of the process
Constructing an I-MR control chart of the output
Performing a Gage R&R study on the measurement system

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Collecting VOC and converting those needs into specific, measurable CTQ characteristics is a core Define activity that links customer needs to project metrics. Why the others are wrong: **B** RTY is a Define/Measure yield metric, not the act of translating customer needs; **C** control charts are a Control-phase monitoring tool; **D** Gage R&R is a Measure-phase study of measurement-system variation, not VOC translation.

questions.stem: A project charter is being assembled. Which element of a Lean Six Sigma project charter states the measurable gap between current and desired performance that the project will close?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** The problem statement quantifies the gap between current and desired performance (what, where, when, how big) without presuming a cause or solution. Why the others are wrong: **A** the timeline schedules the work; **B** the team roster lists who is involved, not the performance gap; **D** the sponsor's name identifies leadership support, none of which states the measurable problem.

questions.stem: A factory produces 1,000 units. 950 pass final inspection on the first attempt with no rework. What is the first-pass yield (FPY) of this step?
questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** First-pass yield is the proportion of units that pass without rework: 950 / 1,000 = 0.95, or 95%. Why the others are wrong: **A** 5% is the defect (fallout) rate, the complement of FPY, not the yield itself; **B** 50% ignores the actual counts entirely; **C** 99.5% would imply only 5 defects, not 50.

questions.stem: A quality manager sorts defect categories by frequency on a bar chart and finds that two of nine categories account for about 80% of all defects. Which principle and tool is being applied?

options.text: The central limit theorem, to justify a normal distribution
Pareto analysis (the 80/20 rule), to focus on the vital few categories
Gage R&R, to separate repeatability from reproducibility

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A Pareto chart orders categories by frequency to reveal the 'vital few' (often ~80% of impact from ~20% of causes), directing improvement effort. Why the others are wrong: **A** the central limit theorem concerns the distribution of sample means; **C** Gage R&R analyzes measurement-system variation; **D** poka-yoke is an error-proofing control technique, not a prioritization chart.

questions.stem: A team begins the Measure phase by creating a high-level diagram that captures Suppliers, Inputs, Process, Outputs, and Customers on a single page. Which tool are they building?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** SIPOC (Suppliers, Inputs, Process, Outputs, Customers) is a high-level map that frames process scope and is a staple early-Measure tool. Why the others are wrong: **B** a control chart monitors variation over time; **C** a scatter plot shows the relationship between two variables; **D** a histogram displays the distribution of a single variable, none of which captures the S-I-P-O-C structure.

questions.stem: In a Measurement System Analysis, several operators measure the same parts with the same gage and obtain noticeably different readings from one another. Which component of measurement variation does this operator-to-operator difference represent?
questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Variation between different operators (appraisers) measuring the same parts is reproducibility. Why the others are wrong: **A** stability is drift in the measurement system over time, not appraiser-to-appraiser difference; **B** repeatability is variation when the same operator measures the same part repeatedly with the same gage; **C** linearity is bias change across the measurement range.

questions.stem: A bathroom scale consistently reads 3 pounds heavier than a certified reference weight, every single time. Which measurement-system property is deficient?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A consistent offset from the true value is bias, a lack of accuracy. Why the others are wrong: **A** precision concerns spread/consistency of repeated readings, and the scale is consistent; **C** repeatability is good because each reading is the same; **D** resolution is the smallest increment the device can display, which is not the issue described.

questions.stem: For a data set, the mean, median, and mode are all equal and the data form a symmetric bell shape. Which distribution does this describe?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A symmetric, bell-shaped curve with mean = median = mode is the normal distribution, the foundation for many Six Sigma statistics. Why the others are wrong: **A** a uniform distribution is flat, not bell-shaped; **B** in a right-skewed distribution the mean exceeds the median; **D** an exponential distribution is strongly right-skewed and not symmetric.

questions.stem: A process is centered and in statistical control. Its specification limits are 6 sigma apart on each side of the mean (total spread tolerance ±6σ). Approximately what is the process capability index Cp?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Cp = (USL − LSL) / 6σ. If the tolerance spans ±6σ (a total of 12σ), then Cp = 12σ / 6σ = 2.0, the capability of a true Six Sigma process. Why the others are wrong: **B** Cp = 1.0 means the tolerance equals 6σ total (a 3-sigma process); **C** 0.5 means the spread is twice the tolerance (incapable); **D** 6.0 confuses the sigma level with the index value.

questions.stem: A process has Cp = 1.5 but Cpk = 0.8. What does the gap between these two indices indicate?

options.text: The process is perfectly centered and highly capable
The process spread is acceptable, but the process is off-center relative to the specification limits
The process has too few data points to assess

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Cp ignores centering while Cpk penalizes it; Cpk well below Cp means the spread is fine but the mean is shifted toward one specification limit. Why the others are wrong: **A** a centered process would have Cpk ≈ Cp, not a large gap; **C** capability indices describe the process, not measurement bias (that is an MSA concern); **D** the indices say nothing about sample size adequacy.

questions.stem: A cross-functional team brainstorms potential causes of a defect and organizes them onto a diagram with major branches labeled Man, Machine, Method, Material, Measurement, and Environment. Which tool are they using?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** The 6M branches (Man, Machine, Method, Material, Measurement, Environment) are the classic categories of a fishbone (Ishikawa) cause-and-effect diagram. Why the others are wrong: **A** a run chart plots a metric over time; **B** a value stream map traces material and information flow with time data; **D** a box plot summarizes a distribution's quartiles, none of which use 6M cause branches.

questions.stem: In a Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA), the Risk Priority Number (RPN) used to rank failure modes is calculated as the product of which three ratings?
questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** RPN = Severity × Occurrence × Detection; higher products flag failure modes for priority action. Why the others are wrong: **A** mean, range, and sample size are statistical quantities unrelated to RPN; **B** cost and generic frequency are not the FMEA rating scales; **C** probability × impact × schedule is closer to generic risk scoring, not FMEA's three factors.

questions.stem: A team is assessing an attribute (pass/fail) measurement system rather than a continuous one. Which two studies or metrics are appropriate for this discrete, attribute data? (Select two.)

options.text: An attribute agreement analysis comparing appraisers' pass/fail ratings to a known standard
Percent agreement (and a kappa statistic) between and within appraisers
A continuous Gage R&R reported as %study variation of a measured dimension
A Cpk computed from variable measurement data

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Attribute (pass/fail) measurement systems are evaluated with attribute agreement analysis and percent-agreement/kappa statistics comparing appraisers to each other and to a standard. Why the others are wrong: **C** a continuous Gage R&R applies to variable (measured) data, not pass/fail judgments; **D** Cpk is a capability index for continuous data, not an attribute MSA method.

questions.stem: Before a team reports process capability (Cp/Cpk), what must first be true of the process for those capability numbers to be meaningful?

options.text: The process must be stable / in statistical control (only common-cause variation present)
The process must have exactly 30 data points
The process must already meet a Cpk of 2.0
All special-cause variation must be intentionally introduced

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Capability indices assume a stable, predictable process; if special causes are present (process out of control), Cp/Cpk are not trustworthy because the process behavior is not predictable. Why the others are wrong: **B** there is no fixed 30-point requirement for capability to be valid; **C** meeting Cpk 2.0 is a result, not a precondition; **D** special causes should be removed, not introduced, before assessing capability.

questions.stem: In hypothesis testing, what does the null hypothesis (H0) typically assert?

options.text: There is a significant difference between the groups
There is no difference or no effect (e.g., the means are equal)

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** The null hypothesis is the statement of 'no difference / no effect' that the test seeks to disprove; the alternative claims a difference exists. Why the others are wrong: **A** sample-size adequacy relates to power, not the null statement; **B** asserting a significant difference is the alternative hypothesis (Ha), not H0; **D** normality is a separate distributional assumption checked before choosing a test.

questions.stem: A test is run at a significance level of α = 0.05 and produces a p-value of 0.02. What is the correct decision?

options.text: Increase α to 0.10 so the result becomes non-significant
Fail to reject the null hypothesis, because the p-value is positive
Accept the null hypothesis as definitively true
Reject the null hypothesis, because the p-value is less than α

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** When the p-value (0.02) is below the chosen α (0.05), the result is statistically significant and you reject the null hypothesis. Why the others are wrong: **A** changing α after seeing the data to manipulate the conclusion is improper; **B** a small p-value leads to rejection, not failure to reject; **C** statistics never 'prove' the null true — you only fail to reject it.

questions.stem: A team concludes there is a real improvement when in fact the process did not change. In hypothesis-testing terms, which error have they committed, and which risk does it correspond to?

options.text: A Type II error, corresponding to beta (β) risk — failing to reject a false null
A Type I error, corresponding to alpha (α) risk — rejecting a true null hypothesis
A sampling error caused by too large a sample
A measurement bias detected by Gage R&R

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Declaring an effect that does not exist is rejecting a true null hypothesis — a Type I error, whose probability is alpha (the producer's/false-alarm risk). Why the others are wrong: **A** a Type II error (beta) is missing a real difference, the opposite mistake; **C** the error is a wrong conclusion, not simply a large sample; **D** Gage R&R addresses measurement-system variation, not hypothesis-test decision errors.

questions.stem: A Green Belt wants to compare the mean cycle time of two independent production lines, and the cycle-time data are continuous and approximately normal. Which hypothesis test is most appropriate?

options.text: A one-way ANOVA across five lines

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Comparing the means of two independent, normally distributed continuous samples is the textbook use of a two-sample t-test. Why the others are wrong: **B** a chi-squared test analyzes categorical/count relationships, not two means; **C** Mann-Whitney is the non-parametric alternative used when normality fails; **D** one-way ANOVA compares three or more group means, more than the two lines here.

questions.stem: A team needs to compare the mean output of four different machines simultaneously using continuous, normal data. Which test avoids inflating the Type I error rate that would result from running many separate t-tests?

options.text: A series of pairwise two-sample t-tests with no adjustment

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** ANOVA tests whether three or more group means differ in a single test, controlling the overall Type I error that multiple separate t-tests would inflate. Why the others are wrong: **A** a paired t-test compares two related measurements, not four independent machines; **B** running many unadjusted t-tests inflates the family-wise alpha — the exact problem ANOVA solves; **C** chi-squared goodness-of-fit examines categorical distributions, not several means.

questions.stem: A team must compare the central tendency of two independent samples, but the data are heavily right-skewed and clearly non-normal even after inspection. Which test is the appropriate non-parametric choice?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The Mann-Whitney U test compares two independent samples without assuming normality, making it the right tool for non-normal data. Why the others are wrong: **A** the two-sample t-test assumes approximate normality, which is violated; **C** ANOVA also assumes normality and compares three or more groups; **D** regression models a relationship between variables, not a two-group central-tendency comparison.

questions.stem: A quality analyst wants to know whether defect type (scratch, dent, crack) is associated with the production shift (day, evening, night). Both variables are categorical. Which test should be used?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A chi-squared test of independence evaluates whether two categorical variables (defect type and shift) are associated using a contingency table of counts. Why the others are wrong: **A** a paired t-test compares means of continuous data from matched pairs, not categorical associations; **B** a two-sample t-test compares the means of a continuous measurement across two groups, not the association between two categorical variables; **D** Pearson r measures the linear relationship between two continuous variables, not categories.

questions.stem: According to the central limit theorem, what happens to the distribution of sample means as the sample size increases, even when the underlying population is non-normal?

options.text: The distribution of the sample means approaches a normal distribution
The variance of individual observations approaches zero
The sample mean always equals the median

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The central limit theorem states that the sampling distribution of the mean tends toward normal as n grows, regardless of the population's shape — which underpins many Six Sigma inference methods. Why the others are wrong: **B** the population's own distribution does not change; **C** individual-observation variance is unchanged (only the standard error of the mean shrinks); **D** mean and median coincide only for symmetric distributions, not as a CLT consequence.

questions.stem: While studying a process, an analyst stratifies output by machine, operator, and time of day to see which family of variation contributes most. Which Analyze technique is this?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Multi-vari analysis graphically partitions variation into families (positional, cyclical, temporal) to point at the dominant source before deeper testing. Why the others are wrong: **A** a control plan documents how to sustain a process in Control; **C** SIPOC scopes the process at a high level; **D** poka-yoke is an error-proofing technique, none of which decompose variation families.

questions.stem: A simple linear regression of cure time (x) on bond strength (y) returns a coefficient of determination R² = 0.81. How should this be interpreted?

options.text: The slope of the regression line is 0.81
Cure time causes 81% of all defects
About 81% of the variation in bond strength is explained by cure time
81% of the data points fall exactly on the line

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** R² is the proportion of variation in the response (y) explained by the predictor(s); 0.81 means cure time accounts for about 81% of the variation in bond strength. Why the others are wrong: **A** R² is not the slope (a separate coefficient); **B** correlation/regression does not by itself prove causation; **D** R² is not the fraction of points lying exactly on the line.

questions.stem: A correlation analysis between two process variables yields a Pearson correlation coefficient r = -0.92. What does this value indicate?

options.text: That one variable causes the other to fall
A strong negative linear relationship — as one variable increases, the other tends to decrease

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** r ranges from -1 to +1; -0.92 is close to -1, indicating a strong negative (inverse) linear relationship. Why the others are wrong: **A** correlation measures association, not causation; **B** -0.92 is strong, not weak, and negative, not positive; **C** an r near zero would indicate no linear relationship, unlike -0.92.

questions.stem: After fitting a regression model, an analyst plots the residuals against the fitted values and against run order. What is the primary purpose of this residual analysis?

options.text: To check whether model assumptions hold (random scatter, constant variance, independence) and the model fits well
To increase the R² of the model automatically
To determine the sample size for the next study
To prove the predictor causes the response

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Residual plots are diagnostics; randomly scattered residuals with constant spread and no pattern over run order support the assumptions of independence, constant variance, and an adequate model form. Why the others are wrong: **B** examining residuals does not by itself raise R²; **C** sample-size planning is a separate exercise; **D** good residuals support model adequacy but do not establish causation.

questions.stem: A team builds a model in which a single response is predicted from three input variables — temperature, pressure, and concentration — fitted simultaneously. Which technique is being used?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Modeling one response from two or more predictors at once is multiple linear regression. Why the others are wrong: **A** a one-sample t-test compares a single mean to a target, not a multi-input model; **B** simple linear regression uses only one predictor; **D** Pareto analysis prioritizes categories by frequency and is not a predictive regression model.

questions.stem: Before rolling a promising solution out to the entire operation, a Green Belt runs it on a single line for two weeks to confirm it works and to surface unintended consequences. What is this step called, and why is it done?

options.text: A hypothesis test — to set the project's alpha risk
A control chart — to monitor the rollout statistically
A SIPOC — to redefine the process scope
A pilot — to validate the solution on a small scale and reduce the risk of a full-scale failure

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Piloting tests an improvement on a limited scale to confirm benefits and uncover side effects before committing to a costly full implementation. Why the others are wrong: **A** a hypothesis test analyzes data, it is not a small-scale rollout; **B** a control chart monitors stability but is not the act of trialing a solution; **C** SIPOC scopes a process in Define/Measure.

questions.stem: Count data (defects per unit) violate the normality assumption needed for a planned analysis. Which approach is a standard way to make such data more suitable for normal-theory methods?

options.text: Delete every value above the mean
Apply a data transformation (for example, a Box-Cox or square-root transformation)
Round all values to the nearest ten
Switch the response and predictor variables

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Transformations such as Box-Cox or square-root reshape skewed/count data toward normality so normal-based tests and models can be applied. Why the others are wrong: **A** deleting data above the mean discards valid information and biases results; **C** rounding does not fix non-normality and loses precision; **D** swapping variables changes the question being asked, not the distribution's shape.

questions.stem: A scatter plot of two process variables shows a clear curved (U-shaped) pattern rather than a straight-line trend. What does this most likely indicate about the relationship?

options.text: The relationship is non-linear, so a curved model may fit better than a straight line
There is no relationship between the variables
The Pearson correlation r is definitely +1
The variables are perfectly, linearly related

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A pronounced curved pattern signals a non-linear relationship that a straight-line fit would misrepresent; a curvilinear or polynomial model is more appropriate. Why the others are wrong: **B** a clear curved pattern is a relationship, just not linear; **C** Pearson r measures linear association and would be low for a symmetric U-shape, not +1; **D** the shape is curved, contradicting a perfect linear relationship.

questions.stem: A 95% confidence interval for a process mean is reported as 12.4 to 13.6 units. Which statement correctly interprets this interval?

options.text: The sample mean has a 5% chance of being wrong
95% of all individual measurements fall between 12.4 and 13.6
There is a 95% chance the next single unit measures between 12.4 and 13.6
We are 95% confident the true population mean lies between 12.4 and 13.6 units

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** A 95% confidence interval is a range that, under repeated sampling, would contain the true population mean 95% of the time; it is an estimate of the mean, not of individual values. Why the others are wrong: **A** misstates the concept — the confidence level refers to the procedure, not a single sample mean being 'wrong'; **B** and **C** describe the spread of individual observations (a prediction/tolerance interval), not a confidence interval for the mean.

questions.stem: A team is selecting among candidate improvement solutions generated in the Improve phase. Which two criteria are most appropriate for prioritizing which solution to pilot? (Select two.)

options.text: The solution's expected impact on the project Y (the CTQ being improved)
The effort, cost, and feasibility required to implement the solution
Which solution was proposed by the most senior person in the room
Which solution uses the largest number of statistical tools

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Solutions are prioritized on benefit (impact on the Y/CTQ) versus effort/cost/feasibility — the classic impact-effort trade-off. Why the others are wrong: **C** deferring to seniority is authority bias, not data-driven selection; **D** the number of statistical tools used is irrelevant to a solution's value or practicality.

questions.stem: A team installs a fixture that physically prevents a part from being inserted in the wrong orientation, so the error simply cannot occur. Which Lean control technique is this?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Poka-yoke is mistake-proofing — designing the process or fixture so a defect cannot be made or is immediately obvious. Why the others are wrong: **A** a Pareto chart prioritizes problems but prevents nothing physically; **C** a hypothesis test analyzes data; **D** a box plot summarizes a distribution, none of which physically block an error.

questions.stem: On a control chart, a single point falls outside the upper control limit and several points trend steadily upward. What does this signal?

options.text: That the specification limits are too wide
Normal common-cause variation requiring no action
The presence of special-cause (assignable) variation that should be investigated
That the measurement system has perfect repeatability

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A point beyond a control limit and a sustained trend are out-of-control signals indicating special-cause variation that warrants investigation. Why the others are wrong: **A** control limits come from process data, not specification limits, so this is not a spec-width issue; **B** common-cause variation stays within the limits with no patterns, unlike this chart; **D** the chart shows process behavior, not measurement-system repeatability.

questions.stem: A team monitors a continuous critical dimension by taking a subgroup of five measurements every hour. Which pair of variable control charts is the standard choice for this situation?

options.text: An I-MR chart (individuals and moving range)

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** For continuous data collected in small subgroups (here n = 5), the Xbar-R chart pair tracks the subgroup mean and the within-subgroup range. Why the others are wrong: **B** a P chart is for the proportion of defective units (attribute data); **C** a U chart is for defects per unit (attribute data); **D** an I-MR chart is used when data are individual measurements with a subgroup size of one, not subgroups of five.

questions.stem: A process is monitored for the proportion of defective units in samples whose sizes vary from day to day (pass/fail inspection). Which attribute control chart is appropriate?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A P chart plots the proportion defective and accommodates varying subgroup sizes, which is exactly this pass/fail, variable-n situation. Why the others are wrong: **A** Xbar-S is for continuous data in larger subgroups; **C** I-MR is for individual continuous measurements; **D** a C chart counts defects per unit with a constant sample size, not the proportion defective with varying n.

questions.stem: A team wants a control chart that is especially sensitive to small, sustained shifts in the process mean (for example, a drift of less than one sigma) that a standard Shewhart chart may be slow to catch. Which charts are designed for this purpose?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** CuSum (cumulative sum) and EWMA (exponentially weighted moving average) charts accumulate information across points, making them far more sensitive to small, sustained mean shifts than a single-point Shewhart chart. Why the others are wrong: **A** a Pareto chart prioritizes categories; **B** an NP chart tracks the count of defectives, not small mean drift; **D** SIPOC is a high-level process map, neither of which is a small-shift detection chart.

questions.stem: A team uses cards that travel with containers; when a container is emptied, its card authorizes replenishment of exactly that quantity, limiting work-in-process. Which Lean control is described?
questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Kanban uses signal cards to pull replenishment only when stock is consumed, capping work-in-process and supporting just-in-time flow. Why the others are wrong: **A** a t-test compares means, none of which is a pull-signal inventory control; **B** a fishbone diagram organizes potential causes; **C** a histogram shows a distribution.

questions.stem: At project closure, a Green Belt documents the key process inputs to monitor, their control limits, the measurement method, sampling frequency, and the reaction plan if a metric goes out of control. Which Control-phase deliverable is this?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A control plan lists what to monitor, the limits, the measurement method, the sampling plan, and the reaction plan to sustain the gains after the project ends. Why the others are wrong: **B** the project charter launches the project in Define; **C** a VOC table captures customer needs in Define; **D** an FMEA assesses failure-mode risk in Measure/Analyze, not the ongoing monitoring plan.

questions.stem: Place the five phases of the Six Sigma DMAIC improvement methodology in their correct order, from first to last.
questions.explanation: The correct DMAIC sequence is Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control. You first Define the problem, goal, and customer requirements; then Measure to baseline the current process with valid data; then Analyze the data to identify and verify the root causes (the vital few x's); then Improve by developing, piloting, and implementing solutions; and finally Control to sustain the gains with monitoring and a control plan. Analyzing before measuring or improving before analyzing would mean acting without the data and validated causes each later phase depends on.

questions.stem: A control plan proposes adding 100% automated inspection to catch a rare defect. A cost-benefit analysis shows the inspection's annual cost far exceeds the cost of the defects it would prevent. What does sound Control-phase practice suggest?

options.text: Abandon the control plan entirely because controls are optional
Always implement the most expensive control available for maximum safety
Weigh the control's cost against the benefit and choose a more cost-effective control when the cost outweighs the value
Ignore cost because quality improvements never need financial justification

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Control selection should be justified by cost-benefit analysis; when a control costs more than the value it delivers, a more economical control (e.g., mistake-proofing or sampling) is the sounder choice. Why the others are wrong: **A** controls are needed to sustain gains, so abandoning the plan is wrong; **B** defaulting to the most expensive control ignores the analysis; **D** Six Sigma explicitly ties improvements to financial benefit, so cost cannot be ignored.

questions.stem: In the original Six Sigma belt structure, which role is typically a full-time change agent who leads multiple complex projects, mentors Green Belts, and reports improvement results to leadership?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A Black Belt is a full-time, project-dedicated practitioner who leads cross-functional DMAIC projects and coaches Green and Yellow Belts. Why the others are wrong: **A** a Yellow Belt is an entry-level team member with basic awareness, not a full-time leader; **C** the Process Owner owns the process day-to-day and receives the improved process, but does not lead the methodology; **D** a Champion is a senior sponsor who removes barriers and selects projects, not the hands-on project leader.

questions.stem: A Lean team redesigns a clinic so that a patient moves from check-in to triage to exam to checkout in one continuous, uninterrupted sequence with no batching or waiting between steps. Which core Lean principle does this best illustrate?

options.text: Increasing batch sizes to gain economies of scale
Maximizing machine utilization at every station
Building large buffers between every step

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Making value move through the process one unit at a time without stops is the Lean principle of continuous flow, which shortens lead time and exposes waste. Why the others are wrong: **A** larger batches add inventory and waiting, the opposite of flow; **B** chasing local machine utilization often creates overproduction and queues, harming overall flow; **C** buffers between steps are inventory waste that flow seeks to eliminate.

questions.stem: An order-entry team logs that a customer's request waits in a queue for two days before anyone begins processing it. Under the eight wastes of Lean, this idle queue time is best classified as which waste?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Time during which work sits idle waiting for the next step, approval, or resource is the waste of Waiting. Why the others are wrong: **A** overprocessing is doing more work or adding more precision than the customer requires; **B** transportation is unnecessary movement of materials or information, not idle time; **D** defects are errors that require rework, not a queue delay.

questions.stem: Customer demand for a product is 480 units per day and the line runs one 8-hour (480-minute) shift with no planned downtime. What is the takt time the process must meet?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Takt time = available production time / customer demand = 480 minutes / 480 units = 1 minute per unit, the rhythm at which the process must produce to meet demand. Why the others are wrong: **B** 480 minutes per unit inverts the calculation and ignores demand; **C** 8 minutes per unit uses hours instead of minutes; **D** 60 units per minute is a rate of production, not takt time, and is numerically wrong.

questions.stem: A team bounds a project by explicitly listing which parts of the process are in scope and which are out of scope, along with the process start and end points and deliverables. Which Define artifact does this describe?

options.text: A project scope statement (in-scope and out-of-scope boundaries)

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Stating what is in and out of scope, the process start/end points, and the deliverables defines the project scope and guards against scope creep within the charter. Why the others are wrong: **A** an FMEA assesses failure-mode risk in Measure/Analyze; **C** a control chart monitors stability in Control; **D** a Gage R&R evaluates measurement-system variation in Measure, none of which bound project scope.

questions.stem: A four-step process has step yields of 0.90, 0.95, 0.98, and 0.99 (first-pass, no rework). Approximately what is the rolled throughput yield (RTY) of the overall process?

options.text: About 95.5% (the average of the step yields)
About 83% (the product of the step yields)
About 382% (the sum of the step yields)

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** RTY is the product of the individual first-pass step yields: 0.90 x 0.95 x 0.98 x 0.99 is approximately 0.83, or 83%. Why the others are wrong: **A** taking only the best step ignores losses at the other steps; **B** averaging the yields is not how RTY compounds across sequential steps; **D** summing yields is meaningless and exceeds 100%.

questions.stem: A unit can have defects in any of 5 opportunities. Over 200 inspected units, the team finds 30 total defects. What is the defects per unit (DPU) for this process?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** DPU = total defects / total units = 30 / 200 = 0.15 defects per unit. Why the others are wrong: **A** 0.03 divides defects by opportunities-times-units (that is the defect rate per opportunity, not DPU); **C** 6.67 inverts the ratio (units per defect); **D** 30 is the raw defect count, not a per-unit rate.

questions.stem: When evaluating which Lean Six Sigma project to charter, which two characteristics make a project a strong candidate for the DMAIC approach? (Select two.)

options.text: The root cause of the problem is unknown and must be discovered through data
The problem is linked to a measurable gap that affects customer CTQs or cost
The solution is already known and just needs to be installed
The project has no clear metric and is mainly a matter of opinion

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** DMAIC fits problems whose causes are unknown and must be found with data and that tie to a measurable gap in a CTQ, quality, or cost outcome. Why the others are wrong: **C** if the solution is already known, just-do-it implementation is more appropriate than a full DMAIC investigation; **D** a problem with no measurable metric cannot be baselined or validated and is a poor Six Sigma candidate.

questions.stem: A data set of repair times is right-skewed by a few very long jobs. Which measure of central tendency is least distorted by these extreme high values and best represents the typical job?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** The median is the middle value and is resistant to outliers, so it best represents the center of skewed data. Why the others are wrong: **A** the mean is pulled toward the long tail by extreme values; **B** the range is a measure of spread, not central tendency, and is highly sensitive to extremes; **D** the standard deviation measures dispersion, not the typical value.

questions.stem: For a normal distribution, approximately what percentage of the data falls within plus or minus two standard deviations of the mean (the empirical rule)?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Under the empirical (68-95-99.7) rule, about 95% of normally distributed data lies within plus or minus two standard deviations of the mean. Why the others are wrong: **A** 68% corresponds to plus or minus one standard deviation; **C** 99.7% corresponds to plus or minus three standard deviations; **D** 50% corresponds only to one side of the mean (the median split), not plus or minus two sigma.

questions.stem: A part measures 110 mm. The process mean is 100 mm and the standard deviation is 5 mm. What is the Z-score (standardized value) of this part?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Z = (x - mean) / standard deviation = (110 - 100) / 5 = 2.0, meaning the part is two standard deviations above the mean. Why the others are wrong: **B** 0.5 inverts the ratio (sigma over the deviation); **C** 10 is the raw difference in mm, not standardized by sigma; **D** -2.0 has the wrong sign because the value is above, not below, the mean.

questions.stem: In a Gage R&R study, a key reported metric is the number of distinct categories (ndc). What does an ndc of at least 5 indicate about the measurement system?

options.text: The gage can reliably distinguish 5 or more distinct groupings of parts across the observed range
The process has exactly 5 special causes

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The number of distinct categories estimates how many non-overlapping groups of part values the measurement system can reliably tell apart; a value of 5 or more is generally considered adequate. Why the others are wrong: **B** ndc is a resolution metric, not a count of special causes; **C** it is not a tally of operator disagreements; **D** it is unrelated to how many parts were sampled.

questions.stem: A continuous Gage R&R reports that the measurement system consumes 32% of the total study variation (%R&R). Per common AIAG guidelines, how should this gage be judged?

options.text: Unacceptable; the measurement system needs improvement (over 30%)
Perfect, because higher %R&R is always better
Irrelevant, because %R&R does not assess a gage

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Under common AIAG guidance, %R&R under 10% is acceptable, 10-30% is marginal (conditionally acceptable), and over 30% is unacceptable; 32% means the gage needs improvement. Why the others are wrong: **A** 32% is far above the under-10% acceptable band; **C** higher %R&R means more measurement noise, which is worse, not better; **D** %R&R is precisely the metric used to judge a measurement system.

questions.stem: A team maps a process and records the value-added time as 12 minutes while the total lead time through the process is 240 minutes. What is the process cycle efficiency (PCE)?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Process cycle efficiency = value-added time / total lead time = 12 / 240 = 0.05, or 5%, a typical sign that most time is non-value-added waiting. Why the others are wrong: **B** 20% would require a value-added time of 48 minutes; **C** 50% would require 120 minutes of value-added time; **D** 95% inverts the relationship and would describe a near-perfect flow, not this case.

questions.stem: A team must report capability for a pass/fail (attribute) characteristic where each unit is judged defective or not. Which capability measure is appropriate for this discrete data?

options.text: Cpk computed from the subgroup ranges
A defect rate expressed as DPMO or a process Z (sigma level)
The standard deviation of the measurement gage

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** For attribute (defective/not) data, capability is summarized by the defect proportion converted to DPMO or an equivalent process sigma (Z) level, not by variable indices. Why the others are wrong: **A** Cpk requires continuous measurements and within-subgroup spread, which pass/fail data lack; **C** correlation describes the relationship between two continuous variables; **D** gage standard deviation is an MSA quantity, not a capability statement.

questions.stem: A team is building a detailed process map and wants to flag every step that the customer would not be willing to pay for. Which classification should those steps receive?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Steps a customer would not pay for and that do not transform the product are non-value-added (waste) and are targeted for elimination or reduction. Why the others are wrong: **A** value-added steps physically transform the product into something the customer values; **C** a control limit is a statistical boundary on a control chart, not a process-step category; **D** a CTQ is a measurable customer requirement, not a classification of a process step.

questions.stem: A Green Belt wants to test whether the mean fill weight of a bottling line differs from the labeled target of 500 g, using one sample of continuous, normal data. Which test is appropriate?

options.text: A one-sample t-test against the target of 500 g

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Comparing one sample mean to a known target value with continuous, normal data is the textbook one-sample t-test. Why the others are wrong: **A** a chi-squared test analyzes categorical counts, not a mean versus a target; **B** a two-sample t-test compares two groups, but here there is one group versus a fixed target; **C** Kruskal-Wallis is a non-parametric test for three or more groups.

questions.stem: The same operators are timed performing a task before and after training, giving two measurements on each operator. To test whether training changed the mean time, which test correctly accounts for the paired structure?

options.text: A paired t-test on the before-minus-after differences

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Two measurements on the same subjects are dependent, so a paired t-test on the within-subject differences is correct and removes between-operator variation. Why the others are wrong: **A** a two-sample t-test assumes independent groups and would ignore the pairing, losing power; **C** ANOVA compares three or more independent groups; **D** chi-squared goodness-of-fit examines categorical distributions, not paired means.

questions.stem: A team must compare the central tendency of cycle times across four suppliers, but the data are clearly non-normal and cannot be transformed. Which test is the appropriate non-parametric choice for three or more groups?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Kruskal-Wallis is the non-parametric analog of one-way ANOVA, comparing the central tendency of three or more independent groups without assuming normality. Why the others are wrong: **A** ANOVA assumes approximate normality, which is violated here; **B** Mann-Whitney handles only two groups, not four; **D** a paired t-test compares two related measurements and assumes normality.

questions.stem: A team suspects two production lines differ in consistency, not in average. Before comparing variances they confirm both samples are approximately normal. Which test directly compares the variability (spread) of the two normal samples?

options.text: An F-test for equality of two variances

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** An F-test compares the variances (spreads) of two normally distributed samples, addressing differences in consistency rather than averages. Why the others are wrong: **A** a two-sample t-test compares means, not spread; **C** a chi-squared test of independence examines association between categorical variables; **D** correlation measures the linear relationship between two variables, not a difference in variability.

questions.stem: Two analysts test the same true difference. Analyst A uses n = 30 and analyst B uses n = 300, all else equal. How does the larger sample size affect the test's ability to detect the real difference?

options.text: It increases statistical power (reduces beta risk), making a true difference easier to detect
It increases the probability of a Type I error above alpha
It guarantees the null hypothesis is true
It has no effect on the test's power

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Larger samples reduce the standard error and raise statistical power (1 - beta), so a real effect is more likely to be detected. Why the others are wrong: **B** alpha (Type I risk) is set by the analyst and is not inflated by larger n; **C** sample size cannot make the null true; **D** power clearly rises with sample size, so claiming no effect is wrong.

questions.stem: When the goal is to test whether the observed frequencies of a single categorical variable match an expected distribution (for example, defects spread evenly across four machines), which test applies?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A chi-squared goodness-of-fit test compares observed category counts to an expected distribution to see whether they agree. Why the others are wrong: **A** a two-sample t-test compares two means of continuous data; **B** regression models a relationship between continuous variables; **D** a paired t-test compares two related continuous measurements, none of which test category-count fit.

questions.stem: A Green Belt plans a one-way ANOVA to compare several group means. Which two assumptions should be checked for the ANOVA results to be valid? (Select two.)

options.text: The residuals are approximately normally distributed
The group variances are approximately equal (homogeneity of variance)
Every group must contain exactly the same categorical labels
The response variable must be a proportion between 0 and 1

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** ANOVA assumes approximately normal residuals and roughly equal variances across groups (plus independent observations). Why the others are wrong: **C** groups are defined by different factor levels, not identical labels; **D** ANOVA compares means of a continuous response and does not require the response to be a proportion.

questions.stem: An analyst reports a 95% confidence interval for the difference between two process means as -1.2 to 3.8. At alpha = 0.05, what does this interval imply about the difference?

options.text: The means differ significantly, because the interval is wide
The difference is not statistically significant, because the interval contains zero
The null hypothesis is proven true

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A 95% confidence interval for a difference that includes zero means zero is a plausible difference, so we fail to reject the null at alpha = 0.05 (not significant). Why the others are wrong: **A** interval width reflects precision, not significance; an interval spanning zero is not significant regardless of width; **C** failing to reject does not prove the null true; **D** the interval describes the mean difference, not measurement bias.

questions.stem: A simple linear regression yields the equation Y = 50 + 4X, where X is temperature in degrees C and Y is yield. How should the slope of 4 be interpreted?

options.text: When X is zero, Y is 4
For each one-degree increase in temperature, predicted yield increases by 4 units
The model explains 4% of the variation in yield

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The slope is the change in the predicted response per one-unit change in the predictor, so each one-degree rise in temperature raises predicted yield by 4 units. Why the others are wrong: **A** the value of Y when X is zero is the intercept (50), not the slope; **C** the slope is not the correlation coefficient, which is bounded between -1 and 1; **D** the slope is not R-squared, which measures explained variation.

questions.stem: In a regression output, the predictor 'pressure' has a coefficient with a p-value of 0.001 while 'humidity' has a p-value of 0.42 (alpha = 0.05). What is the most reasonable conclusion?

options.text: Pressure is a statistically significant predictor; humidity is not
Both predictors are significant because both have a p-value
Humidity is the stronger predictor because its p-value is larger
Neither predictor matters because regression cannot test significance

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A coefficient p-value below alpha (pressure at 0.001) indicates a statistically significant predictor, while a p-value above alpha (humidity at 0.42) does not. Why the others are wrong: **B** simply having a p-value does not make a term significant; humidity exceeds alpha; **C** a larger p-value indicates weaker, not stronger, evidence; **D** regression coefficients are routinely tested for significance via their p-values.

questions.stem: A team runs a designed experiment varying two factors, each at a low and high setting, and tests all combinations to study their effects on yield. What type of experiment is this?

options.text: A 2-level full factorial design of experiments (DOE)

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Testing every combination of two factors each at two levels is a 2-level full factorial DOE, which also reveals interactions between factors. Why the others are wrong: **A** OFAT changes one factor while holding others fixed and cannot detect interactions; **C** a control chart monitors stability over time, it is not an experiment; **D** SIPOC is a high-level process map, not a designed experiment.

questions.stem: In a designed experiment, the effect of temperature on yield is large when pressure is high but negligible when pressure is low. What does this pattern indicate?

options.text: A significant interaction effect between temperature and pressure
That temperature has no main effect at all
That the experiment must be discarded
That the two factors are perfectly correlated predictors

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** When the effect of one factor depends on the level of another, the factors interact; that is the definition of an interaction effect. Why the others are wrong: **B** temperature does have an effect (large at high pressure), so a no-main-effect claim is unsupported; **C** an interaction is a valid, useful finding, not grounds to discard the study; **D** an interaction between controlled factors is not the same as collinearity (correlation) between predictors.

questions.stem: After validating root causes, a team generates many possible solutions and then plots each on a 2x2 grid of benefit versus implementation effort to decide what to pilot first. Which decision aid are they using?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Plotting solutions by benefit against effort on a 2x2 grid is an impact-effort (prioritization) matrix that highlights high-benefit, low-effort 'quick wins'. Why the others are wrong: **B** a control chart monitors process stability, not solution selection; **C** a normal probability plot checks distribution shape; **D** a Gage R&R report evaluates measurement-system variation.

questions.stem: An analyst extrapolates a regression model fitted on temperatures of 20-40 degrees C to predict yield at 90 degrees C. Why is this extrapolation risky?

options.text: The modeled relationship may not hold outside the range of the observed data
It automatically lowers the model's R-squared to zero
Extrapolation always reverses the sign of the slope
Regression equations cannot produce predicted values

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A regression model is only validated within the range of the data used to fit it; outside that range the relationship can change shape, so extrapolated predictions are unreliable. Why the others are wrong: **B** extrapolating does not recompute or zero out R-squared; **C** the slope does not automatically flip when extrapolating; **D** regression equations do produce predictions — the issue is their validity far outside the data.

questions.stem: A regression model includes several predictors and the analyst worries some predictors are themselves highly correlated, inflating the standard errors of the coefficients. What is this condition called?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** When predictors are strongly correlated with one another, the model suffers multicollinearity, which inflates coefficient standard errors and makes individual effects hard to interpret. Why the others are wrong: **B** heteroscedasticity is non-constant residual variance, a different diagnostic; **C** a Type I error is a hypothesis-testing mistake, not a predictor-correlation issue; **D** reproducibility is a measurement-system (MSA) concept.

questions.stem: Before scaling a piloted solution to the full operation, which two questions should the Improve-phase pilot be designed to answer? (Select two.)

options.text: Does the solution actually move the project Y (improve the CTQ) as expected?
Does the solution create unintended side effects or new problems elsewhere?
Which team member proposed the idea?
How many statistical tools can be applied to the data?

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** A pilot confirms the solution delivers the intended improvement in the Y and surfaces unintended consequences before a costly full rollout. Why the others are wrong: **C** who proposed the idea is irrelevant to validating its effect; **D** the count of statistical tools used has no bearing on whether the solution works.

questions.stem: On a control chart, control limits are most commonly set at how many standard deviations from the center line?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Shewhart control charts place the upper and lower control limits at plus or minus 3 sigma from the center line, balancing false alarms against detection. Why the others are wrong: **A** plus or minus 1 sigma would trigger far too many false signals; **B** plus or minus 2 sigma is sometimes used as a warning zone but is not the standard control limit; **D** plus or minus 6 sigma describes a capability target, not chart control limits.

questions.stem: A fundamental distinction in SPC is between control limits and specification limits. Which statement correctly describes the difference?

options.text: Control limits come from the process's own data (the voice of the process); specification limits come from customer/engineering requirements (the voice of the customer)
Control limits and specification limits are the same thing
Specification limits are always set at plus or minus 3 sigma of the process
Control limits are chosen by the customer's tolerance

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Control limits are computed from process variation (voice of the process) to detect special causes, while specification limits express customer/engineering tolerances (voice of the customer). Why the others are wrong: **B** they are conceptually distinct and should never be placed on the same chart as equivalents; **C** specification limits derive from requirements, not automatically from plus or minus 3 sigma; **D** control limits come from process data, not the customer's tolerance.

questions.stem: A team counts the number of defects (not defectives) on each inspected unit, and the area of opportunity is constant from unit to unit (for example, scratches per painted panel). Which attribute control chart fits this count data?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A C chart plots the count of defects per inspection unit when the area of opportunity (sample size) is constant. Why the others are wrong: **B** a P chart tracks the proportion of defective units, not a count of defects; **C** an Xbar-R chart is for continuous data in subgroups; **D** an NP chart counts the number of defective units with a constant sample size, not defects per unit.

questions.stem: A team monitors a continuous critical dimension using subgroups of size 10 collected each shift and wants the within-subgroup spread charted accurately. Which variable control chart pair is preferred over Xbar-R for these larger subgroups?

options.text: Xbar-S charts (subgroup average and standard deviation)

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** For larger subgroups (commonly n of about 10 or more), the Xbar-S chart uses the subgroup standard deviation, which estimates spread more efficiently than the range used in Xbar-R. Why the others are wrong: **B** a P chart is for proportion defective (attribute data); **C** I-MR is for individual measurements (subgroup of one); **D** a U chart is for defects per unit (attribute data).

questions.stem: On a control chart, eight consecutive points fall on the same side of the center line even though none crosses a control limit. Per standard run rules, how should this be treated?

options.text: As an out-of-control signal indicating a likely shift in the process mean
As routine common-cause variation requiring no action
As proof the measurement system is broken
As evidence the specification limits are too tight

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A run of eight (or more) consecutive points on one side of the center line is a recognized run-rule signal of a process shift, even with no point beyond the limits. Why the others are wrong: **B** such a non-random pattern is special-cause, not common-cause, variation; **C** a run rule signals process behavior, not a broken gage; **D** control-chart signals are independent of specification limits.

questions.stem: As part of sustaining gains, a team posts a single board at the work cell showing real-time output, quality, and the day's targets so anyone can see process status at a glance. Which Lean control concept does this represent?

options.text: Visual management (a visual control / andon board)

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Displaying status, targets, and abnormalities so they are immediately visible to everyone is visual management (visual controls), a key Lean technique for sustaining performance. Why the others are wrong: **B** a t-test is a statistical comparison, not a workplace control; **C** a box plot summarizes a distribution; **D** regression models relationships, none of which is the visual-control concept described.

questions.stem: At the end of a project, the Green Belt formally transfers ownership of the improved process, the control plan, and the monitoring responsibilities to the person who runs the process day-to-day. To whom is this handoff made?
questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Control-phase closure hands the improved process and its control plan to the Process Owner, who is accountable for running and sustaining it after the team disbands. Why the others are wrong: **A** the customer receives the output but does not own and monitor the internal process; **B** an external auditor verifies compliance but does not own day-to-day operation; **C** a Master Black Belt mentors and governs methodology, not routine process ownership.

questions.stem: A robust Control-phase reaction plan accompanies a control chart. Which two elements should the reaction plan specify? (Select two.)

options.text: The specific corrective actions to take when an out-of-control signal occurs
Who is responsible for responding and how the response is documented
The marketing budget for the product line

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** A reaction plan states what to do when the process signals out-of-control and who must act and record the response, so the control is actually sustained. Why the others are wrong: **C** a marketing budget is unrelated to reacting to a process signal; **D** an executive's travel schedule has no place in a process reaction plan.

questions.stem: Which company is generally credited with originating the Six Sigma methodology in the 1980s, coining the term and using it to drive large-scale quality improvement?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Motorola developed and trademarked Six Sigma in the mid-1980s, with engineer Bill Smith credited for the underlying work. Why the others are wrong: **A** Toyota originated the Toyota Production System and Lean, not Six Sigma; **C** Ford adopted quality methods but did not create Six Sigma; **D** General Electric famously popularized and scaled Six Sigma under Jack Welch in the 1990s but did not originate it.

questions.stem: A service team logs the time staff spend re-keying the same customer information into three separate systems, work that adds no value the customer would pay for. Under the eight wastes of Lean, which waste is this re-entry an example of?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Doing more work than the customer requires — such as redundant re-keying of the same data — is overprocessing. Why the others are wrong: **B** transportation is the unnecessary movement of materials or product, not duplicated effort; **C** inventory is excess stock or work-in-process held in queues; **D** overproduction is making more or sooner than demand requires, not repeating a processing step.

questions.stem: Lean thinking is often summarized by five core principles. Which two of the following are among those five Lean principles? (Select two.)

options.text: Specify value from the perspective of the end customer
Establish pull so work is triggered by downstream demand
Maximize batch sizes to gain economies of scale
Inspect finished goods to remove all defects before shipping

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Womack and Jones's five Lean principles are define value, map the value stream, create flow, establish pull, and pursue perfection — so specifying customer value and establishing pull are both included. Why the others are wrong: **C** maximizing batch size works against flow and pull and tends to create overproduction and inventory waste; **D** relying on end-of-line inspection is a detection approach Lean seeks to design out, not a core principle.

questions.stem: An organization launches a project to design a brand-new product and production process to Six Sigma quality levels from scratch, rather than improving an existing one. Which methodology is most appropriate for this design-focused effort?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** DMADV (Define, Measure, Analyze, Design, Verify) — part of Design for Six Sigma — is used to create new products or processes that meet customer requirements from the outset. Why the others are wrong: **A** DMAIC improves an existing process rather than designing a new one; **B** 5S is a workplace-organization method, not a design framework; **D** firefighting is ad hoc problem-solving, the opposite of a structured design methodology.

questions.stem: During Define, a team gathers input from frontline employees about safety concerns and friction in the daily workflow, separate from what external customers say. Which 'voice' does this employee input represent?
questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Input gathered from the people who perform the work is the Voice of the Employee (VOE). Why the others are wrong: **A** VOC captures the needs of external customers, not internal staff; **B** Voice of the Process is the statistical performance the process actually delivers, expressed through data and control charts; **C** VOB reflects the needs of the business such as cost, growth, and shareholder value.

questions.stem: Cost of Quality (CoQ) is commonly grouped into four categories: prevention, appraisal, internal failure, and external failure. Which two of these are the failure-cost categories that make up the Cost of Poor Quality? (Select two.)

options.text: Internal failure costs (scrap and rework found before delivery)
External failure costs (warranty claims and returns after delivery)
Prevention costs (training and error-proofing to avoid defects)
Appraisal costs (inspection and testing to detect defects)

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** COPQ's failure costs split into internal failure (defects caught before reaching the customer, e.g., scrap and rework) and external failure (defects that reach the customer, e.g., warranty and returns). Why the others are wrong: **C** prevention costs are spent to stop defects from occurring and are a cost of good quality, not a failure cost; **D** appraisal costs are inspection/testing costs to find defects, also a category of conformance cost rather than failure.

questions.stem: A process produces 2,000 units; each unit has 4 opportunities for a defect, and inspectors find 24 defects in total. What is the defects per million opportunities (DPMO)?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** DPMO = defects / (units x opportunities) x 1,000,000 = 24 / (2,000 x 4) x 1,000,000 = 24 / 8,000 x 1,000,000 = 3,000. Why the others are wrong: **B** 12,000 ignores the 4 opportunities and divides by units alone; **C** 3.0 omits the scale-up to one million; **D** 6,000 doubles the defect count or halves the opportunities, neither of which matches the data.

questions.stem: A team translates a broad customer desire — 'I want fast service' — into a measurable specification: 'orders fulfilled within 5 minutes, 95% of the time.' Which Define tool helps decompose a general need down to such specific, measurable requirements?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A Critical-to-Quality (CTQ) tree breaks a broad customer need down into drivers and finally into specific, measurable requirements. Why the others are wrong: **B** an I-MR chart monitors a process over time and is a Control tool; **C** Gage R&R evaluates measurement-system variation in Measure; **D** a scatter diagram explores the relationship between two variables, not the decomposition of a customer need.

questions.stem: A team needs a measure of variability expressed in the same units as the data (e.g., millimeters) so it can be compared directly to the process mean and specification limits. Which statistic should they report?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The standard deviation is the square root of the variance and is expressed in the original units of the data, so it compares directly with the mean and specifications. Why the others are wrong: **A** variance is in squared units, which do not match the data scale; **C** the mode is a measure of central tendency, not spread; **D** the coefficient of variation is a unitless ratio (std dev / mean), not a same-units measure.

questions.stem: For a normal distribution, approximately what percentage of observations falls within plus or minus one standard deviation of the mean, according to the empirical (68-95-99.7) rule?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Under the empirical rule, roughly 68% of a normal distribution lies within plus or minus one standard deviation of the mean. Why the others are wrong: **A** 50% corresponds to one side of the mean (the median split), not the +/-1σ band; **C** about 95% lies within +/-2σ; **D** about 99.7% lies within +/-3σ.

questions.stem: In a Measurement System Analysis, the same operator measures the identical part ten times with the same gage and gets slightly different readings each time. Which component of measurement variation does this within-operator scatter represent?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Variation when one operator measures the same part repeatedly with the same gage is repeatability (equipment variation). Why the others are wrong: **A** reproducibility is the variation between different operators measuring the same parts; **B** linearity is how bias changes across the measurement range; **D** stability is drift in the measurement system over time, not scatter within a single repeated set.

questions.stem: A characteristic has only an upper specification limit (USL) of 50; there is no lower limit. The process mean is 44 and the standard deviation is 2. Which calculation gives the appropriate capability index?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** For a one-sided upper spec, CPU = (USL − mean) / 3σ = (50 − 44) / (3 × 2) = 6 / 6 = 1.0. Why the others are wrong: **B** dividing by 6σ is the two-sided Cp form and is not used for a one-sided distance from the mean; **C** omitting the 3σ denominator gives a Z-style distance, not a capability index; **D** using a nonexistent lower limit of 0 measures the wrong side of the distribution.

questions.stem: A team reports both Cp/Cpk and Pp/Ppk for the same process. Conceptually, what distinguishes the 'P' (performance) indices from the 'C' (capability) indices?

options.text: Performance indices (Pp/Ppk) use the overall, long-term standard deviation, while capability indices (Cp/Cpk) use the within-subgroup, short-term standard deviation
Performance indices ignore the specification limits entirely
Capability indices are only valid for attribute data
Performance indices are computed without any standard deviation

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Pp/Ppk are based on the overall (long-term) standard deviation of all the data, whereas Cp/Cpk use the within-subgroup (short-term) sigma; the gap reflects between-subgroup shift and drift. Why the others are wrong: **B** both index families use the specification limits; **C** capability indices apply to continuous data, not attribute data; **D** performance indices absolutely require a standard deviation — just the overall one.

questions.stem: A digital caliper displays readings only to the nearest 1 mm, but the tolerance the team must control spans just 2 mm. Why is this gage's resolution (discrimination) a problem?

options.text: The gage is biased high by 1 mm
The increment is too coarse to distinguish parts within the tolerance, hiding real variation
The gage has poor reproducibility between operators
The gage drifts over time and is unstable

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Resolution (discrimination) is the smallest increment a device can read; when that increment is large relative to the tolerance, the gage cannot tell parts apart and masks real variation. Why the others are wrong: **A** describes bias, a constant offset, not coarse increments; **C** describes appraiser-to-appraiser variation; **D** describes drift over time, not the resolution issue.

questions.stem: A continuous-improvement team walks the factory floor and draws the physical travel path of a single part as it moves from station to station, revealing excessive back-and-forth movement. Which diagram are they creating?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A spaghetti diagram traces the actual physical movement of a product, person, or information through a process to expose transportation and motion waste. Why the others are wrong: **B** a histogram shows the distribution of a single variable; **C** a Pareto chart ranks categories by frequency; **D** a control chart monitors a metric over time, none of which map a physical travel path.

questions.stem: On a value stream map, a team records both the time a part is actively worked (processing time) and the much larger total elapsed time from start to finish. Which metric captures that total elapsed time, including all waiting?

options.text: Lead time (total cycle time through the stream)

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Lead time is the total elapsed time a unit spends moving through the value stream, including processing plus all waiting and queue time — distinct from cycle time, which measures only the active processing at a step. Why the others are wrong: **A** value-added time counts only the steps that transform the product as the customer requires; **C** takt time is the pace of customer demand, not elapsed time through the stream; **D** setup time is the time to change a process over between products.

questions.stem: A team fails to detect a real reduction in defect rate because their sample was too small, so they wrongly keep the null hypothesis of 'no change.' Which error is this, and which risk does it correspond to?

options.text: A Type I error, corresponding to alpha (α) risk
A Type II error, corresponding to beta (β) risk
A measurement error detected by Gage R&R
A sampling bias corresponding to the confidence level

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Failing to reject a null hypothesis that is actually false — missing a real effect — is a Type II error, whose probability is beta (the consumer's risk). Why the others are wrong: **A** a Type I error (alpha) is the opposite mistake: declaring an effect that does not exist; **C** Gage R&R addresses measurement-system variation, not a hypothesis-test decision error; **D** the confidence level relates to interval estimation, not the missed-detection error described.

questions.stem: A study is designed with statistical power of 0.90. What does this power value represent?

options.text: The probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis (detecting a real effect)
The probability of a Type I error
The probability that the sample mean equals the population mean

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Power equals 1 − β, the probability of correctly rejecting the null when a real effect of a given size exists; 0.90 means a 90% chance of detecting that effect. Why the others are wrong: **B** the Type I error probability is alpha, set independently of power; **C** power is not about a single sample mean matching the population; **D** alpha is the significance level (false-alarm rate), distinct from power.

questions.stem: A Green Belt only cares whether a new method makes cycle time shorter than the current mean — a change in the opposite direction is of no interest. How should the alternative hypothesis be framed?

options.text: As a two-tailed (two-sided) test, μ ≠ μ0
As a one-tailed (one-sided) test, μ < μ0
As a test of variance rather than the mean
As a null hypothesis of inequality

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** When only a decrease matters, a one-tailed (one-sided) alternative such as μ < μ0 puts all the rejection region on the side of interest and gives more power to detect it. Why the others are wrong: **A** a two-tailed test splits attention across both directions, which is unnecessary here; **C** the question concerns the mean, not the variance; **D** the null is a statement of no difference/equality, not the alternative of inequality.

questions.stem: The standard deviation of a population is fixed. How does the standard error of the mean change as the sample size n increases?

options.text: It increases in proportion to n
It stays exactly the same as the population standard deviation
It decreases, shrinking in proportion to the square root of n
It becomes negative for large n
